headline: MIT Technology Review has set out why experts disagree on whether freely downloadable AI models do more good than harm.
score_reason: Useful context on a live policy debate, but it is an explainer with no new event or evidence, so it stays at the curator's 5.
importance_line: The argument shapes whether governments and AI labs restrict or promote freely downloadable models, which affects researchers, businesses that run models on their own hardware and anyone exposed to AI-assisted hacking, though the piece is an explainer built on expert opinion, not new evidence, and it notes that Nvidia and Anthropic have commercial interests in the outcome.
summary: In an explainer published on 13 Oct 2026, MIT Technology Review says open models, whose internal settings (weights) anyone can download, tend to be cheaper, easier for researchers to study and a check on the power of a few AI labs, but they carry no prompt filters, cannot have access revoked and can be retrained to drop their safety training. The piece, which follows Anthropic's late-September report calling the Chinese open model GLM-5.3 a major cyberattack risk, adds that closed models are also misused and that ideas such as staged release and tamper-resistant training do not yet withstand all attacks.
